title: Antonelli explains approach to starting at the back in Monza
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli has outlined his mindset as he prepares to start from the back in front of his home crowd at the Italian Grand Prix, with the Mercedes driver also explaining whether he will sacrifice his Qualifying to support team mate George Russell.

Despite arriving at the event with a 59-point lead in the championship, it was confirmed ahead of the weekend that Antonelli will serve a grid penalty at Monza due to a planned engine change, posing an extra challenge for the Italian on Sunday.

However, when speaking to the media on Thursday ahead of his local Grand Prix, Antonelli spoke of the “opportunity” he could take from the circumstances as well as admitting that his grid position helps to alleviate some of the pressure from racing at home.

“It feels very special [to be leading the championship at my home race],” he explained. “Definitely a lot different compared to last year, and I'm very much looking forward to this weekend, despite starting from the back.

“But it's also a big opportunity I have, and very much looking forward to it. I think it's going to be very enjoyable – I will be able to enjoy it much more than what I did previously, and hopefully we can still do a great race.

“I think [starting from the back] in some ways helps to release pressure, although I'd very much rather fight for pole and start there at the front. But in some way it makes me a bit more relaxed going into the weekend. I think also that's why I'm going to be able to enjoy more the driving and the weekend itself.

“And of course it's a different opportunity, it's an opportunity to try something different during the weekend, a different work method as well in Free Practice especially, because we have the chance to do so. So yeah, I think it's going to a very interesting weekend.”

In terms of what he believes might be possible from his starting position, Antonelli said: “In an ideal world, I think realistically top five you can do well, but it's all driven by also your pace, how fast you are, what's the gap between cars.

“We might be really quick, but Ferrari, McLaren or Red Bull, they might be very close [and then] it’s probably not enough to catch them during the race, but we'll see. Definitely I feel very free mentally going into this weekend. I'm actually very excited, very much looking forward to it, but with no real pressure.”

Given his impending penalty, Antonelli was also quizzed on whether he might do anything to support fellow Mercedes driver Russell – such as providing a tow – during Qualifying.

“It has been discussed with the team, and yes, we have agreed on a few things,” the 20-year-old said. “Let's see how the session develops, but if the team will ask me to do so, I will do it.”

Overall, the championship leader conceded that he is carrying a very different mindset into the weekend compared to how he felt one year earlier, having experienced a difficult spell across the European leg of his rookie season.

“[The main change this year is] that I don't have to prove as much as I had to do last year,” Antonelli explained. “Last year, obviously I was coming from a difficult period as well, and I felt like I had to prove myself, to prove that I could belong in F1.

“I feel like also that increased a lot the pressure on myself, and that made me drive very tense. I wasn’t really enjoying as well the time in the car. This year, obviously I'm lucky to have a great car, but as well, also the year of experience makes a huge difference.

“I feel much more mature, much more in control of the situation. And obviously then also when you get the good results in, it's always one less thing to prove and I've proven that I can win, I've proved that I can perform, and that's why coming into this weekend, yes it's my home race, it's great, but it is another race like the others.”

title: Hamilton ‘strongly believes’ in Ferrari’s victory chances
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton was all smiles as the F1 paddock reconvened at the Autodromo Nazionale Monza on Thursday, with the Ferrari driver hoping that an engine update will boost his and the team’s Italian Grand Prix chances.

Hamilton started the Monza weekend in style with a statement arrival outside the paddock gates – turning up in a classic Ferrari F40 that he recently acquired while wearing a stylish black suit and tan overcoat.

After posing in front of the world’s photographers, Hamilton headed to the pre-event press conference, during which he fielded plenty of questions about how special it is to represent the Scuderia on their home soil, as well as what might be possible on track over the next three days.

“I mean, it’s the best feeling to be a Ferrari driver,” said Hamilton. “It’s such an honour and a privilege to arrive in Italy at this iconic race with the most iconic and best team in the world.

“It’s really phenomenal to experience it for the second year in a row, and it still feels new, so it’s not something you can get used to.”

Asked about another engine upgrade that Ferrari are set to introduce this weekend, and whether it will be enough to put him in contention for victory, Hamilton added: “Every little helps; every little helps.

“I think up until this point of the year we’ve been losing… even in the last race, on such a short circuit, we were losing four tenths a lap through the race, so that’s a huge deficit and we’ve carried that through the year to this point.

“What I can say is I really, really am proud of when I go back to the factory and I see how hard everyone is working, that they’re really just heads down. Everyone’s so enthusiastic.

“I see a different focus this year to last year. Last year I felt like there wasn’t really a North Star, and we were kind of... I think doing the best we could, but not really knowing where exactly we were trying to aim for.

“Now we have a North Star, we know where we need to work towards, and I think they’ve [the team at the factory] done a tremendous job to really pull together and deliver.

“This is a step forward. It’s not the whole gap that we need, but we knew that would be the case. But to see bits coming each weekend, adding to the car, it’s exciting to see that we are pushing. I strongly still believe that we’ve got what it takes to win.”

After a difficult first season at Ferrari, Hamilton admitted to arriving at this year’s event aware there could be “a first ahead of me” – in terms of potentially becoming an Italian Grand Prix winner at the wheel of a Ferrari, as well as moving clear of Michael Schumacher with six Monza triumphs.

Pushed on his comments about challenging for the victory this weekend, Hamilton added: “Well, my point was that I strongly believe that the team has what it takes to win.

“At this level, how close it is up front… I think for us to win this weekend, and in any weekend, it takes the whole collective to come together. It’s not just one thing; everything has to flow from the beginning.

“The pressure’s high. You want to deliver for the team. There’s all those people that are at the factory, and many of them will come to this race. The Tifosi come out in huge numbers, the passion is unmatched, and you want to deliver for them as well.

“My mum’s here this weekend. She’s never experienced… I don’t think she’s been to Monza, but also particularly on a Ferrari weekend, and I wanted her to experience that and bring any of the lucky dust she can bring.”

title: How every corner at Monza got its name
excerpt:
As the oldest circuit on the F1 calendar, the Autodromo Nazionale Monza holds decades of memories – but how well do you know the history of its corner names? Let’s take a look at the origins of each one…

Turns 1/2 – Prima Variante

The Temple of Speed was first constructed in 1922 and has undergone several changes, primarily to improve safety. Prima Variante, which has a no-nonsense translation of ‘first chicane’, was added when the circuit underwent refurbishment in 1972 to reduce the intensely high speeds.

It was previously known as the Variante del Rettifilo, roughly meaning ‘chicane of the straight’ as it was located in the middle of the original start/finish straight, but this title was shed for good when the turn was reprofiled again in 2000.

Turn 3 – Biassono

This sweeping right-hander used to be called Curva Grande (‘great curve’) due to its shape, but the aforementioned alterations in the early 1970s led to its new identity of Biassono, sharing its name with a local town.

Turns 4/5 – Seconda Variante

Next up is another aptly-named sequence of turns called Seconda Variante, or ‘second chicane’, that was created in further modifications made in 1976 to lessen the danger of the track – the extra run-off areas here are another indication of that goal.

This is a site of high drama, such as the 1995 collision between championship rivals Damon Hill and Michael Schumacher, but offers a fantastic spot for overtaking. It’s also sometimes referred to as Curva della Roggia after a nearby stream.

5 storylines we’re excited about ahead of the Italian GP

Turns 6/7 – Lesmo 1 & 2

Born the Curva della Querce (‘curve of the oaks’) due to the forest that envelops the circuit, this pair of right-handers were renamed Lesmo 1 and 2 for another local town. There are additional theories that its origin traces back to a family that lived in the region, or has a connection to the Greek island of Lesbos.

In years gone by, Lesmo 2 – formerly labelled Curva dei 100 Metri (‘100 metre curve’) for the short distance that separated the entry point from the exit, and the Curva del bosco dei Cervi (‘curve of the deer forest’) – was remarkably fast, with only the most courageous entering the turn at speeds of up to 300kph.

More adjustments in 1994 meant that its rapid nature was somewhat subdued, but it’s still a crucial spot for drivers hoping to set up an overtake at the next corner.

Turns 8/9/10 – Variante Ascari

After a very slight left-hand bend known as the Curva del Serraglio, which isn’t an official corner but commemorates a royal hunting lodge that stood close by, the straight leads into the final chicane called Variante Ascari.

It remembers Italian racing legend Alberto Ascari, a two-time World Champion who was tragically killed in an accident at the Monza Circuit in 1955. Prior to the dedication, the series of corners was named Curva del Platano (‘plane tree curve’) or Curva del Vialone (‘avenue curve') because it passed over the large access road to the track.

Turn 11 – Curva Alboreto

Last but by no means least is Curva Alboreto, still often called Parabolica – the 180 degree right-hander that looks like a mathematical curve called a parabola. It’s seen plenty of memorable moments and carries a fearsome reputation as a result, with bravery and commitment once again being key here.

A few years ago, the turn was renamed Curva Alboreto after former driver Michele Alboreto, who competed in F1 between 1981 and 1994.

title: What does the Italian GP ‘heat hazard’ declaration mean?
excerpt:
Another ‘heat hazard’ has been declared by Formula 1’s governing body, the FIA, ahead of the Italian Grand Prix weekend. But what exactly does it mean for the teams and the drivers at Monza? F1.com offers an all-in-one reminder…

What is a ‘heat hazard’ declaration?

For some background, following the particularly high temperatures and humidity experienced over the 2023 Qatar Grand Prix weekend, the FIA began an analysis into how similar situations could be managed in the future.

Ahead of the 2025 season, it was confirmed that a ‘heat hazard’ can be declared if pre-weekend weather forecasts predict temperatures of 31 Celcius or above at some point during a Sprint or Grand Prix.

Teams are notified of the declaration by the FIA, as they have been in Italy, and subsequently need to fit a ‘Driver Cooling System’.

Just how hot will it be in Italy?

As touched on above, F1’s Italian Grand Prix takes place at the Autodromo Nazionale Monza, near the city of Milan – one of many regions in Europe gripped by heatwaves in recent times.

“In accordance with Article B1.5.10 of the FIA F1 Regulations, having received a forecast from the Official Weather Service predicting that the Heat Index will be greater than 31.0°C at some time during the Race at this Competition, a Heat Hazard is declared,” read a note from FIA F1 Race Director Rui Marques to teams on Thursday morning.

Indeed, all three days of action at Monza are set to feature air temperatures above 30 Celsius, and as high as the mid-30s, meaning a sweaty weekend ahead for the drivers.

What is the ‘Driver Cooling System’?

In short, this is defined as a system with the “sole purpose” of providing additional cooling for drivers under a ‘heat hazard’ scenario.

Several components are involved, including a pump, plumbing and thermal store, with cold fluid generated by the system delivered to the drivers through a special fireproof vest featuring various tubes.

All of the core system components must be fitted to cars, though drivers are currently permitted to choose whether or not they wear the vest itself as work continues on fine-tuning the design.

“Any driver may elect not to wear any items of personal equipment that form part of the Driver Cooling System,” reads Article B1.5.10 of the Sporting Regulations. “In such circumstance, all other components, including any cooling medium of the Driver Cooling System, must be fitted.

“In addition, the difference in mass between the driver’s personal equipment normally used and any items of a driver’s personal equipment that form part of the system must be compensated by the fitting of 0.5kg of ballast in the cockpit.”

What have the drivers said about it?

When a ‘heat hazard’ was last declared at the Austrian Grand Prix, McLaren driver Oscar Piastri confirmed his intention to use the cooling vest, while outlining some of the benefits and areas for improvement.

“I used it a couple of times last year,” he explained. “There’s obviously the risk of if it goes wrong, and if it fails, then it’s worse than not wearing it. I think if you get the system working well, it can help a bit.

“It’s not a complete gamechanger, but when I used it last year it was okay. There are definitely some things that are not perfect with it, but at the end of the day, it’s personal preference.

“We have to add the weight in the car anyway, so if you can get it to work and it cools you down a little bit, then sure.”

Attention now turns to Friday’s first practice session in Italy, where all 22 drivers will have another chance to use the cooling system and vest – should they wish to do so.

title: Facts, stats and trivia ahead of the 2026 Italian Grand Prix
excerpt:
The 2026 Formula 1 season continues this weekend as Monza hosts Round 13 on the calendar, the Italian Grand Prix.

Free Practice 1 and 2 will take place on Friday, September 4, followed by Free Practice 3 and Qualifying on Saturday, September 5, and the Grand Prix itself on Sunday, September 6.

Vital statistics

First Grand Prix – 1950

Track Length – 5.793km

Lap record – 1m 20.901s, Lando Norris, McLaren, 2025

Most pole positions – Lewis Hamilton (7)

Most wins – Michael Schumacher and Lewis Hamilton (5)

Trivia – The Italian Grand Prix has featured on the F1 calendar since the inaugural 1950 season, with Monza home to every race apart from 1980, when Imola played host

Pole run to Turn 1 braking point – 476 metres

Overtakes completed in 2025 – 47

Safety Car probability – 50%*

Virtual Safety Car probability – 38%*

Pit stop time loss – 24.14 seconds

*From the last eight races at Monza

The driver’s verdict

Jolyon Palmer, former Renault F1 driver: Monza is one of a kind on the calendar, yet in many ways is the simplest track. It’s low downforce and all begins with braking into the chicane for Sector 1 and getting your car to stop as nicely as you can for Turn 1 – that’s the key.

In the middle sector, the Lesmos are actually more fun to drive than they look, with a slight camber. You can carry a bit of speed in, pick your line for a little brake and again through Lesmo 2 as well.

Gravel can greet you if you carry too much speed into Turn 8/9/10 at Ascari – the first part of the corner is the crucial area – but it’s quite bumpy as well. Then stay pinned through 9 and 10, if you get 8 right, which takes you to Parabolica or Curva Alboreto (renamed after the late Michele Alboreto).

Sadly, they took away the gravel that was the charm of this final corner, but it’s still a cool challenge – attack it, run right around the outside to carry speed, get on the throttle as soon as possible and charge onto the main straight.

It used to be perilous with the gravel on the outside, whereas now a little bit of the exhilaration is maybe taken away with the tarmac run-off, but it’s still possible to crash and Monza is still a fantastic high-speed circuit.

Everything you need to know about the Monza circuit

Last five Italian GP polesitters

2025 – Max Verstappen (Red Bull)

2024 – Lando Norris (McLaren)

2023 – Carlos Sainz (Ferrari)

2022 – Charles Leclerc (Ferrari)

2021 – Max Verstappen (Red Bull)

Last five Italian GP winners

2025 – Max Verstappen (Red Bull)

2024 – Charles Leclerc (Ferrari)

2023 – Max Verstappen (Red Bull)

2022 – Max Verstappen (Red Bull)

2021 – Daniel Ricciardo (McLaren)

Tyre and strategy insight

“The 5.793 km circuit, featuring 11 corners, is one of the fastest on the Formula 1 calendar, thanks in part to its long straights which, this year, will present an additional challenge for energy management with the new power units,” Pirelli’s weekend preview reads, with the compounds available this weekend being the C3 (as the hard), C4 (as the medium) and C5 (as the soft).

“Team simulations are in fact predicting lap times around two seconds quicker than last year. From a tyre perspective, the front axle should be subjected to lower braking loads, as braking zones are likely to be approached at reduced speeds. By contrast, the rear axle will face greater demands during traction phases, when the full power of the power unit is deployed.

“Braking stability and traction on corner exit, particularly at the First Chicane and Ascari, will be the two key factors in gaining an advantage over rivals on a track that is typically run with a low-downforce aerodynamic set-up, prioritising top speed.

“The circuit generally offers a good level of grip from the opening sessions. No significant modifications have been made since the complete resurfacing carried out in 2024, when a relatively smooth asphalt mixture was laid. This year, the kerbs at Turns 1, 4 and 8 have been rebuilt, while at Turn 5 a gravel area has been replaced with an asphalt run-off section.

“Drivers will likely have to manage rear axle overheating during the race, but degradation should not be severe enough to compromise tyre performance. As a result, a one-stop strategy appears the most likely option for Sunday, despite the fact that overtaking opportunities are far from scarce at Monza.”

Current form

Kimi Antonelli continues to head the drivers’ standings as he arrives into his home race weekend, with the Italian now holding a 59-point margin over Mercedes team mate George Russell and Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton.

The championship leader took second place last time out at the Dutch Grand Prix, but the Silver Arrows left Zandvoort feeling that they need to improve the pace of their car in order to stay in the battle with their competitors.

One of those rivals to make a key step forward recently is McLaren. Lando Norris claimed his second consecutive victory when the season resumed after the summer break, and the Briton will be keen to extend that run this weekend.

Norris currently sits fourth in the World Championship, meaning that he has some ground to make if he is to defend his title – and with the next driver ahead of him being Hamilton, Ferrari will be hoping to put up a fight themselves in front of the adoring Tifosi at Monza.

Red Bull, meanwhile, faced a challenging outing at Zandvoort, with Max Verstappen suffering an early crash while stand-in Liam Lawson did the best he could en route to P7. Can the Milton Keynes-based outfit bounce back at a venue where Verstappen took victory last year?

Elsewhere, points for Alpine in Zandvoort helped the team to close in on Racing Bulls in the scrap over P6 of the Teams' Championship, while Audi made ground by adding to their tally in eighth and Aston Martin were also bolstered by Fernando Alonso’s P9 finish at the Dutch Grand Prix. Who will have the upper hand in the midfield fight this weekend?

Iconic moment

Following that aforementioned note about Monza featuring on the F1 calendar every year bar one since 1950, it comes as no surprise that our archives are filled with unforgettable moments from decades past.

One particularly special weekend at Monza occurred back in 2008, when a rookie by the name of Sebastian Vettel made quite an impression by clinching his debut pole position and race victory during a rain-soaked event.

Just over a year into his full-time F1 career with the Red Bull-backed Toro Rosso team, Vettel mastered the slippery conditions to upset the establishment not only over one lap but also a race distance.

One of the standout underdog results in recent Grand Prix history, it sent Vettel on his way to a glittering career that included 52 more victories and four world titles.

title: Everything you need to know about the Monza circuit
excerpt:
Formula 1 returns to action with the Italian Grand Prix this weekend. But how much do you know about the Autodromo Nazionale Monza? F1.com presents your all-in-one guide…

Key Monza statistics

Circuit length: 5.793km

Number of turns: 11

Number of laps: 53

Race distance: 306.72km

Lap record: 1m 20.901s – Lando Norris (2025)

When was Monza’s first Grand Prix?

Constructed in just 110 days in 1922, the Autodromo Nazionale Monza was the world’s third purpose-built race track, coming after Brooklands in the UK and Indianapolis in the US.

Like those two tracks, the original Monza circuit featured a daunting series of banked curves, as well as much of the ‘outfield’ section that’s still in use today.

Monza opened its doors on September 3 1922, just a week before it hosted that year’s Italian Grand Prix. It was then part of the original F1 calendar in 1950, and has held the Italian Grand Prix every year bar one since.

What’s the circuit like to drive?

Red Bull driver Max Verstappen’s 264kph average speed during his 2025 pole lap (more on that below) should give you some idea of the nature of the track that locals call ‘La Pista Magica’.

Cars are on full throttle for 80% of the lap, and hit their Vmax on the circuit’s 1.1km start/finish straight. From there, they roar off into the historic park section, where a series of big stops into tight chicanes give the brakes a good workout.

So, just how do drivers approach the unique challenge of racing at Monza?

“Monza is one of a kind on the calendar, yet in many ways is the simplest track,” says former Renault F1 driver Jolyon Palmer. “It’s low downforce and all begins with braking into the chicane for Sector 1 and getting your car to stop as nicely as you can for Turn 1 – that’s the key.

“In the middle sector, the Lesmos are actually more fun to drive than they look, with a slight camber. You can carry a bit of speed in, pick your line for a little brake and again through Lesmo 2.

“Gravel can greet you if you carry too much speed into Turn 8/9/10 at Ascari – the first part of the corner is the crucial area – but it’s quite bumpy as well. Then stay pinned through 9 and 10, if you get 8 right, which takes you to Parabolica or Curva Alboreto (renamed after the late Michele Alboreto).

“Sadly, they took away the gravel that was the charm of this final corner, but it’s still a cool challenge – attack it, run right around the outside to carry speed, get on the throttle as soon as possible and charge onto the main straight.

“It used to be perilous with the gravel on the outside, whereas now a little bit of the exhilaration is maybe taken away with the tarmac run-off, but it’s still possible to crash and Monza is still a fantastic high-speed circuit.”

Monza is one of a kind on the calendar, yet in many ways is the simplest track.Jolyon Palmer

Where are the Straight Mode zones and overtake detection?

As a reminder, and as explained in our pre-season summary of regulation changes, Straight Mode is a different aerodynamic configuration that allows cars to reduce their drag, making them more efficient when accelerating up towards top speed.

The rear wing continues to open up a gap – just like it did when drivers used DRS (the Drag Reduction System) in the past – but now the front wing also moves. The uppermost front wing elements drop down at the same time the rear wing’s top element does.

This is a mode that is used on every single lap in dry conditions, in every area that is designated for it. Essentially, the car will adapt between two different configurations depending on where it is on the track, providing maximum downforce in corners but then less drag on straights.

At Monza, there are four designated Straight Mode zones: a run along the start/finish straight, followed by the sections between Turns 3 and 4, Turns 7 and 8, and Turns 10 and 11.

Meanwhile, Overtake Mode replaces DRS and is a new power mode that allows a driver to recharge more electrical energy, and generate an additional electrical power profile, so they can sustain a higher speed for a longer period.

There is one detection point per lap for this mode – expected to be out of the final corner on many occasions, leading onto a long straight – and it will be available to drivers on the following lap as long as they stay within a second of the car in front at that detection point.

The Overtake Detection marker here comes just before the entry to Turn 11, while the Overtake Activation line follows on the exit of that corner, heading onto the start/finish straight.

Five fun facts about the Italian Grand Prix

As referenced above, the Italian Grand Prix has featured on the F1 calendar since the inaugural 1950 season, with Monza home to every race apart from 1980, when Imola played host

Verstappen made history at Monza in 2025 when he set the fastest average speed lap in F1 history during Qualifying (264.682kph)

Monza has the second fewest corners on the F1 calendar with 11 – behind only Austria’s Red Bull Ring (which features 10)

Lewis Hamilton and Michael Schumacher have won the most Italian Grand Prix with five victories each

Ferrari have won the most Italian Grands Prix with 20 victories

title: Max Verstappen provides health update after battling 'awful' illness
excerpt:
Max Verstappen has shared how he is feeling ahead of the Italian Grand Prix, having suffered through illness at the previous round in Zandvoort.

Max Verstappen has confirmed he is fully recovered from the illness that plagued him throughout the Dutch Grand Prix, describing his experience as "awful" in the days before and after the race.

The Red Bull driver was visibly under the weather across the entire Zandvoort weekend, battling flu-like symptoms that left him feeling far from his best.

He qualified seventh for his home race and then saw his afternoon end abruptly on the opening lap when he lost control at the banked final corner on a damp track, spinning hard into the barriers and triggering a red flag.

Speaking to media ahead of the Italian Grand Prix at Monza, Verstappen was asked how he had been feeling in the days after Zandvoort, addressing both the first-lap crash and his illness.

"I felt good in terms of the impact, because it was the SAFER [steel and foam energy reduction] barrier," the Dutchman told media, including RacingNews365.

"So that was the first time that I did that. It actually did its job really well."

Driver

Max Verstappen

Dutch

3

'The whole week in Zandvoort was awful'

While the four-time F1 drivers' champion walked away from the crash unscathed, it was the illness that proved far harder to shake off.

The 28-year-old admitted that the bug lingered well beyond the race weekend itself.

The week-long break between the Dutch and Italian rounds afforded Verstappen the time he needed to get back to full fitness.

"But yeah, I was very ill," the 71-time grand prix winner added. "You appreciate it once you're fully healed, like how good it is to feel like that, because the whole week in Zandvoort was awful.

"And even after Zandvoort, for a few days, I was still not good. So it was actually really nice to have that week to recover and feel better again, because it's been a very long time since I felt like that."

title: Kimi Antonelli confirms Mercedes discussions in George Russell support role
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli has confirmed that talks have been held with Mercedes ahead of this weekend's Italian Grand Prix regarding him supporting George Russell.

The championship leader faces the task of starting his home race from the back of the grid, with the Silver Arrows choosing to fit Antonelli's car with an entirely new power unit.

Antonelli was already on the cusp of a grid drop due to having almost used every engine component within his pool, something he has now exceeded.

Monza was chosen as the best place to take a heavy grid penalty by the Brackley-based operation, due to the expectation that overtaking will be very possible.

It makes qualifying effectively meaningless for Antonelli, with his title rivals having a great chance to reduce the 20-year-old's title advantage.

One of those drivers is Russell, who Antonelli has confirmed he will support in qualifying by offering a tow should the instruction come from Mercedes.

Asked if helping Russell has been discussed with the team, Antonelli told select media, including RacingNews365: "Yeah, it is.

"It has been discussed with the team, and yes, we have agreed on a few things, so let's see how the session develops. But if the team asks me to do so, I will do it.

"I will do it because, yeah, obviously, I will still be happy to get pole, but of course, I'm starting at the back.

"So, if I could do anything to help the team, I will. I will do it."

title: Lewis Hamilton details 'sheer magnitude' of Italian GP pressure as clear target set
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton has set his sights on winning the Italian Grand Prix for the first time as a Ferrari driver this weekend.

The seven-time champion has enjoyed huge success at Monza, winning five times in his career - the joint-most alongside Michael Schumacher.

However, his last win at the venue came eight years ago, while Ferrari has won twice since then with Charles Leclerc, in 2019 and 2024.

Ferrari arrive at the Italian GP this weekend with an upgraded engine as it hopes to get involved in the fight at the front - a mission Hamilton has full faith in.

“I strongly believe that the team has what it takes to win at this level, how close it is at the front,” Hamilton told media including RacingNews365.

“For us to win this weekend, and at any weekend, it takes the whole collective to come together. It's not just one thing; everything has to flow from the beginning.

“And I really thought coming into this weekend, just thinking of the sheer magnitude of the concept that I'm coming to this grand prix... I didn't even know that I was equal with Michael on wins.

“But the thought of that there is a first ahead of me, in a sense of potentially, if you were to win, you go into new territory.

“Winning in Monza for the first time with Ferrari is something I've witnessed Charles win in 2019 when I was on the podium with him.

“To do it while I'm here would be phenomenal. The thought of if I did do that, probably will be the only black driver to ever do that for Ferrari in Italy, probably in history.

“A lot of those thoughts have been through my mind.”

Hamilton has taken to the top step of the podium with Ferrari once already this year, triumphing in Barcelona in emotional circumstances.

A win at Monza would likely match or even exceed the excitement that was felt in June, and Hamilton is feeling the tension rising as he prepares for the first day of on-track action.

“The pressure is high, you want to deliver for the team,” he said.

“All those people at the factory, many of them will get to come to this race. The Tifosi come out in huge numbers, the passion is unmatched, and you want to deliver for them as well.

“And my mum's here this weekend, I don't think she's been to Monza, but also particularly on a Ferrari weekend.

“I wanted her to experience that and bring any of the lucky dust she can bring.”

title: Franco Colapinto highlights F1 'goal' after fresh Alpine deal
excerpt:
Franco Colapinto has outlined his latest F1 goal after securing a drive on the 2027 grid with Alpine.

The deal was announced last week, with Alpine opting to retain an unchanged line-up by keeping Colapinto alongside Pierre Gasly, who is secured on a long-term deal.

Colapinto joined Alpine last year after replacing Jack Doohan just a handful of rounds into the season.

It was a tormenting campaign for the Enstone-based squad as it placed its resources into its 2026 challenger, which has been a regular point-scorer this year.

Colapinto's performances aided the team's decision to keep him for another year, and the Argentine pledged to continue to play his part in pushing the team forward.

“Of course, very happy to continue - very, very happy and grateful to the team that has done an amazing job since I started,“ Colapinto told media including RacingNews365.

“Last year was tricky, this year we have made a big step together as a team, and it's great to continue this journey together and to be able to keep working as a family for next season.

“We have a lot of work to do, and we are going to try hard to keep developing and keep improving as a team, that's the goal for us.”

In contrast to its approach last year, Colapinto has suggested Alpine will not halt the development of its current car in a bid to start next year's campaign in an even stronger position.

As it targets a top five finishing position for the first time since 2022, Colapinto insisted its goal is to end the year as high as it can in the standings.

“It's great to be with the team for another year,” he added. “Of course, we have to keep working a lot.

“We are going to be pushing this year. First, our goal isto finish as high as we can, and then, of course, we want another step for 2027.”

title: Max Verstappen sets fresh Red Bull target after 'disappointing' moment
excerpt:
Max Verstappen has stated that both he and Red Bull must work to ensure the RB22 is fine-tuned to a competitive window at the Italian Grand Prix this weekend.

The Monza Circuit hosts the 13th round of the 2026 F1 campaign this weekend, with Verstappen seeking a return to the podium.

After back-to-back top-three results in Belgium and Hungary, the four-time champion entered his home event in the Netherlands last time out hoping to add to his podium tally.

However, his race ended on the opening lap as he spun in tricky conditions, making heavy contact with the barrier.

It marked an excruciating result for Verstappen, at what was the final Dutch Grand Prix for the foreseeable future.

“Not being able to finish the race in Zandvoort was disappointing,” Verstappen said ahead of the weekend.

“But it was still really special to see the fans at the circuit one last time and thank them for all the memories.”

Verstappen has triumphed at the Italian Grand Prix at Monza on three occasions during his career, including last year's event as he continued to close the gap to McLaren in the championship.

However, the 28-year-old refrained from putting a label on expectations for the weekend ahead, insisting the primary task was getting the car set up in a strong window.

“We are heading to Monza, after a reset, and it is difficult to predict how competitive we will be there,” he said.

“There are a few things we need to work on to be a bit closer to the pace and to make sure balance of the car is right.

“Monza is one of my favourite tracks and I like that it is an old-school, fast circuit; I always enjoy coming here and seeing the passionate fans.

“It is a track that we have typically performed well at before so we will wait and see what is possible."

title: Key F1 supplier 'braking' ground as new challenge intensifies
excerpt:
F1’s new era has presented a serious challenge for Brembo, the brake manufacturer partnering with all Formula 1 teams, while significant preparations are also required for 2027. The Italian company's research, development, and testing department is working at full throttle — all under one roof.

3 September 12:45PM

Preparing for F1's new era, which started this season, was a massive task for Brembo, because braking has become more complex than ever before at the pinnacle of motorsport.

Now, it demands continuous action from the brake manufacturer, connected to all teams, who must simultaneously focus on 2027 whilst meeting the demands of this year.

During an exclusive interview with RacingNews365, Andrea Dellavedova, race engineer for the Italian brand, pointed out that changing the combustion-to-electric power ratio and the timing of the decision intensifies the challenge for Brembo as well.

"Yeah, because now we have done half a year, so we understand more, and we were focusing on some direction. As next year the energy ratio will change, what we learned this year will not be that useful for the new development," he begins.

"This year we already started to think about the 2027 braking system, but now we have to think newly about the system, and we cannot use all the info that we discovered this year for the next one."

As is well known, after lengthy and extensive consultations, the FIA confirmed in June that it will modify the ratio in two steps: it will change to 58:42 for 2027, and then shift to 60:40 for 2028.

"Being in a very fast environment, the more time we have to develop the new system, the better it is. If the communication would happen some weeks before… it's always easier, because we have to design and test the prototype, and then launch the production," Dellavedova adds.

"The time horizon is very short, because the teams need the components for early next year. It's something that takes time, both designing and producing our components. From the design to the production phase, it takes months; it's not something that you can do in weeks, because the process itself of producing the disc and the carbon material is very long, because they have to spend time in the oven, with several processes.

"Also, the calliper itself, they have to spend a lot of time on the machine. Then there is also the testing. Sometimes we do the testing and the production in parallel."

Brembo building on a strong foundation

The task is massive, but Brembo has a strong foundation to build upon: the brand's excellent engineers utilise state-of-the-art infrastructure.

The company's operational and administrative center is located in Kilometro Rosso, Bergamo's science and technology park, while they operate manufacturing and commercial facilities in 18 countries worldwide.

In terms of F1 and motorsport, Curno in Italy, located near the headquarters, is the key plant: this is where the racing technology is created.

"We have several dyno test benches that we use to test the new developments in terms of both materials, geometries and also dimensions of the braking system. They are running 24 hours per day, 6 days per week," says Dellavedova about the "witch's kitchen" in Curno.

According to the Italian engineer, keeping research, design, and development in-house and under one roof provides a major competitive advantage, even in the world of brake development.

"The performance is there with both offices and also the production and testing department," he continues.

"We are very close, so the designer can work on the laptop, design the new component and in a very fast way they just go to the first floor — the dyno test benches are there with the people working directly on the tests, so they have a very fast way of communicating, and also they can physically inspect the products that they are developing."

Although preparing for 2027 is a serious challenge for Brembo, Dellavedova looks to the future with confidence based on their current situation, available capacity, and experience.

He concludes: "In terms of timing, we are in line. In terms of performance, based on our experience, yes, because, of course, we are doing the best that we think will be the best for the next year."

title: Major F1 record predicted to be broken at Italian GP
excerpt:
Aston Martin's chief trackside officer Mike Krack has stated he is expecting a large amount of overtaking at the Italian Grand Prix this weekend.

The 54-year-old went so far as to say that it could set a new record for the highest number of passes in a single race.

The current record was set at the 2023 Dutch Grand Prix, which saw 186 position changes throughout the field during a chaotic event impacted by rain.

This year's F1 cars race somewhat differently compared to challengers from the past, with energy deployment playing a major role following the increase in battery output.

Across the opening events of the year, it was common for cars to be repassed shortly after completing a move due to running out of energy.

With Monza's layout featuring many long straights which could see a repeat of such a situation, Krack is expecting to see many overtakes take place on Sunday.

“It will be an interesting exercise to validate your models, but also to see how operationally you manage it,” Krack told media including RacingNews365.

“It is one side to say the effect big or small, but also you have to be in a position to follow someone.

“So there are quite a lot of restrictions on the energy side this weekend. It will be interesting to see how teams we we go about it, first of all, in free-of-tow deployment, but then also in a tow situation.

“Then also in the race, how easy passing will be, and especially the passing and repassing games. It probably will be a record of all time here, or like MotoGP.”

Monza sits as one of the fastest F1 tracks on the race calendar, with speeds peaking at around 360 km/h in modern times - however, the figures are set to decrease this year.

Should drivers use different energy deployment strategies throughout the upcoming event, Krack admits that it could create a dangerous situation.

“Normally, the deployment profiles converge over a weekend, so I do not expect any major differences.

“But if people deploy completely differently, then there is always a risk.”

title: F1 teams handed 'crucify' warning as Ferrari singled out
excerpt:
Mika Hakkinen has addressed the team orders situation in F1 after the issue came to the fore at Zandvoort.

3 September 11:15AM

Mika Hakkinen has warned F1 teams that fans will turn on them if they impose team orders to shape the title fight, singling out Ferrari's handling of Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc at the Dutch Grand Prix as a case study in indecision.

Mercedes executed a clean driver swap at Zandvoort, instructing George Russell to let Kimi Antonelli through for second place after a late Virtual Safety Car had artificially inverted their positions.

Antonelli, on fresher soft tyres, had been running ahead before the pit sequence and was the faster car. Russell questioned the call but complied; Mercedes locked out second and third behind race winner Lando Norris, and the matter was largely put to bed.

Ferrari's situation was messier. Hamilton, on a better strategy and fresher rubber, caught Leclerc in the middle phase of the race and asked to be let through, but the Scuderia never issued the order.

Instead, the team eventually pitted Leclerc to clear Hamilton's path, but the delay cost Hamilton several seconds, and he finished fourth, less than a second behind Russell, costing him a podium finish. Hamilton was frustrated, suggesting Ferrari should learn from Mercedes' decisiveness.

Hakkinen, speaking to Sky Sports F1, made clear he understood Hamilton's reaction and felt it went beyond mere frustration.

"I think what Lewis experienced in Zandvoort, it was explained from the team why it happened," the two-time F1 drivers' champion said. "Emotions with Lewis' experience were absolutely normal. Maybe it wasn't only emotion, just also common sense, 'We can score more points if you let me overtake!'"

Hakkinen also offered a broader explanation for why drivers so often clash with their teams in these moments, pointing to the information gap between the cockpit and the pit wall.

"But nowadays when I look at grand prix racing from the outside, when I'm in the paddock, it's different. You see much more, you get much more information on what's happening," he said.

"The drivers are getting only a very tiny percentage of the information we get on TV, so when they are following another car, and it doesn't let them overtake, they don't have the information and the calculations that the team have, so then very often you get these kinds of reactions from the drivers, which is very normal."

Driver

Mika Häkkinen

Finnish

A warning for the title fight

It is a nuance that helps explain Hamilton's visible frustration at Zandvoort. Sitting behind Leclerc, aware only that he was faster and losing time, he could not see the broader strategic picture Ferrari was attempting to manage.

That context does not excuse the team's hesitation, Hakkinen suggested, but it does put the driver's reaction into perspective.

The 20-time grand prix winner drew on his own era racing against Michael Schumacher's Ferrari to illustrate how much the sport has changed, and why teams face a far more combustible environment when it comes to managing two drivers.

"The fanbase has changed in Formula 1; the generation is different than in my time," Hakkinen said. "When I was racing against Michael Schumacher when he was at Ferrari, they started doing team orders already at the first race of the season.

"It was very obvious that if one driver is very strong in a team and started to win races and score points, the team is very much aware that if they want to win the world championship, they need to support this one driver 100 per cent.

"That's what Michael Schumacher was able to manage to do with Ferrari when he was racing there.

"We had a little bit of a different philosophy at McLaren. We wanted to give both drivers the same opportunity until the points were at a point that one couldn't catch the other; then the team-mate has to start supporting the leading driver. That was a common-sense operation."

With the championship battle tightening, Hakkinen's central message was clear: the old playbook no longer applies cleanly.

Teams cannot simply install a number one and a number two without consequence, because the modern fanbase will not accept it quietly.

"Now the teams want to win the drivers' championship and the constructors' championship; they want to win both. So it's important that both drivers are getting maximum performance all the time in every race...," he said.

"Which team is going to do this kind of change [implementing team orders], and what are the arguments they are going to give and tell the fans? This is going to be an important factor.

"All these drivers have a huge fanbase these days in the world, and if the team are going to decide one day that this driver is going to be number two, the fans are going to crucify this team."

title: Lando Norris traits highlighted where 'he has improved the most'
excerpt:
McLaren team principal Andrea Stella has highlighted two of the key areas where he feels Lando Norris has improved significantly after thrusting himself back into the picture for this season's F1 drivers' title.

Following a major upgrade on the MCL40 ahead of the Hungarian Grand Prix, Norris has ended his winless drought with back-to-back victories either side of the summer break at the Hungaroring and Zandvoort.

From barely being mentioned as a title contender, Norris is back in the conversation, albeit the Briton still faces a considerable task if he is to retain his championship as he currently trails leader Kimi Antonelli by 83 points.

From Stella's perspective, however, he has enjoyed a different side to Norris of late, in particular after he gave himself a rare pat on the back for his part in achieving victory in the Dutch Grand Prix. Ordinarily, he has been quick to self-criticise.

One of the highlights of Norris' performance was his pass on Antonelli around the outside of Turn 1, notably with Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton also in the equation.

"I would say he is definitely expressing a higher level of assertiveness as he drives," said Stella, speaking to the media, including RacingNews365. "The manoeuvre to pass Antonelli was a really good demonstration of that.

"He is demonstrating more self-confidence, and with self-confidence, it is interesting, and I quite like it.

"Sometimes, self-confidence is not demonstrated by being the most aggressive. Sometimes you are self-confident when you think, 'You know what? I'm not going to fight now because I might lose this fight. It's a very long race. See you at the end of the race'.

"It's this confidence in your means, in your strength that I quite like, which means that sometimes you are the one backing off when the situation becomes too risky. So I do see the self-confidence.

"We need to remember that in both of the last couple of races that he won, he didn't defend the pole position. He was actually second at the end of the first lap.

"But I did not perceive any decay in his confidence. Instead, he was fast and just preparing his opportunity to then cash in on his competitiveness.

"So I think assertiveness and confidence are probably the two characteristics where he has improved the most from a non-technical, non-operational point of view."

Next up for McLaren and Norris is the Italian Grand Prix at Monza on September 6.

title: Ferrari handed 'cautiously optimistic' verdict as Monza pressure cooker awaits
excerpt:
Former IndyCar driver James Hinchcliffe has handed Ferrari and its fans his belief that the Scuderia can be "cautiously optimistic" about this weekend's Italian Grand Prix.

F1's annual visit to Monza represents the biggest weekend of Ferrari's season, with it being the ultimate pressure-cooker event for the Maranello-based outfit.

Ferrari consistently introduces an upgrade package especially for its home race, in pursuit of securing victory at one of the most iconic races on the calendar.

With Ferrari having failed to claim a podium in the last two races, there will be pressure on the team to return to the rostrum at the very least, if not challenge for victory.

A special livery has already been unveiled by Ferrari, while the Italian manufacturer is also introducing its second engine upgrade of the year in pursuit of Mercedes.

Ferrari, and in particular Lewis Hamilton, do remain in the title fight, although a strong result is needed this weekend to keep genuine hopes alive.

Predicting whether Ferrari will perform strongly or not has been a challenge in 2026, with it often performing well at venues where it is expected to struggle, and then doing badly where it is expected to thrive.

Discussing Ferrari's chances this weekend, Hinchcliffe told the F1 Nation podcast: "Well, it's interesting, right? Because they've been competitive at tracks that maybe we weren't expecting them to be, and then vice versa, maybe a little bit off the pace at some tracks that we kind of thought they were going to be right up front.

"I think of Silverstone and even Spa. They were decent, and you're heading to Monza, a big horsepower track. They seem to have found something in that department.

"They always seem to have a little bit of something special there, don't they? I mean, they are usually competitive. Even in seasons when they're not that competitive in other places, they seem to focus.

"It's like they build their car around Monza, and then, okay, we'll figure the rest out as we go. So, I mean, cautiously optimistic for the Tifosi that they can have a strong weekend. Again, they didn't qualify particularly well at Spa, if I remember, but they were decent in the race."

title: FIA declare heat warning for Italian GP as extreme temperatures forecast
excerpt:
The FIA has declared a 'Heat Hazard' for the Italian Grand Prix, the 13th round of the 2026 F1 season.

Temperatures at Monza are forecast to exceed normal early September levels, which typically sit around 25-27°C, prompting the governing body to activate its formal heat-stress protocol ahead of the weekend.

The Heat Hazard framework was introduced for the 2024 season following the harrowing scenes at the 2023 Qatar Grand Prix, where extreme heat and humidity left multiple drivers in serious physical distress.

Esteban Ocon vomited inside his helmet and continued racing, Logan Sargeant was forced to retire on medical grounds, while Lance Stroll and Alex Albon required post-race treatment for heat exhaustion. Several drivers reported being close to blacking out at high speed.

In the aftermath, the FIA formalised a plan to stop such a situation from occurring again in the future, and with the temperature this weekend set to exceed 31.0°C, it has opted to intervene.

For Monza, drivers will benefit from enhanced cooling measures on the grid, including fans, ice vests and shade structures.

Cars are also permitted to run the FIA-approved driver cooling system, which circulates cooled fluid through tubing in a vest worn beneath the race suit to help regulate body temperature during track running.

Use of the system is not compulsory, meaning drivers can choose not to wear it if they prefer. However, those who opt out must carry equivalent ballast so there is no performance advantage from avoiding the additional weight of the cooling equipment.

Post-session medical checks will be mandatory, with dedicated cooling areas available immediately after track running

title: Lando Norris makes huge announcement in fresh career challenge
excerpt:
Lando Norris has announced the formation of his own racing team, which will be set up in the junior categories in 2027.

The reigning world champion confirmed the news on the eve of the Italian Grand Prix as he goes in pursuit of a third successive race win.

Norris' own team will be part of several junior racing series next year, including the FIA Formula 3 Championship, which is a support series at a number of F1 events.

The team, called LN4Fusion, has acquired selected assets from AIX Racing and is also targeting an entry onto the Formula 2 grid, seen as the last stepping stone for drivers hoping to reach F1.

“We've created a racing team, LN4Fusion,” Norris wrote on social media.

“I was lucky enough to achieve my dream and now I want to help others achieve theirs.

“Built with people I trust, people who’ve experienced all levels of motorsport and know exactly what it takes to win. The goal is to become the leading junior single-seater team. We'll be on the grid in Italian F4, FREC, F3, and are working on a place in British F4 and F2.”

Norris has also created his own junior driver programme, offering funding for up-and-coming talents to help them realise their racing dream.

“That’s not all. We’ve also created the LN4 Legacy Programme to fund and support talented young drivers who might otherwise not get the opportunity,” Norris added.

“Giving them the support they need on and off track to have the best chance of success.

“To see this go from an idea to something real is incredible. Huge thanks to everyone who has played a part in making this happen.

“Excited for what's to come. See you on the grid in ’27.”

Norris is not the only current driver with his own team, as Max Verstappen established his own outfit a handful of years ago.

However, while Norris is targeting single-seater competition, Verstappen's squad mainly focuses on GT racing.

title: Ferrari confirm major Monza upgrade in Mercedes pursuit boost
excerpt:
Ferrari team principal Fred Vasseur has confirmed that the Scuderia will introduce its latest engine upgrade at this weekend's Italian Grand Prix.

Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc's SF-26s will be fitted with a second power unit upgrade of the season as part of the Additional Development Upgrade Opportunities (ADUO) scheme, with Ferrari having further opportunities to upgrade its engine next year.

The Maranello-based outfit has historically always introduced a significant upgrade at Monza, with it being the most important event on the calendar for the Scuderia.

With a sea of red awaiting Ferrari in the grandstands, much is expected of Hamilton and Leclerc, especially with the team still having a chance of winning both titles.

For that, a good weekend in Italy is needed for both drivers, who will be wearing special race suits in recognition of Michael Schumacher, while the SF-26 has a one-off livery.

Monza is all about horsepower and top speed, two factors Ferrari has lacked in 2026. The hope will be that the new power unit changes that.

"Monza is always a very special weekend for Ferrari," said Vasseur. "Racing in front of our Tifosi gives the whole team incredible energy and this year there will be an additional emotional dimension as we celebrate Michael Schumacher and the legacy he has left in our company.

"His relentless pursuit of improvement, attention to detail and strong belief in teamwork are values that remain key to us today. On the performance side, we are introducing an updated power unit as part of the development opportunities available under ADUO.

"It represents a step in the right direction and as we know this year is very much about marginal gains. Monza is a demanding circuit and the field is extremely close, and our priority will be to execute every aspect of the weekend as well as possible, from Friday onwards.

"We want to draw extra motivation from the passion of our home crowd and give our Tifosi a strong weekend."

title: McLaren preach caution ahead of F1 season-defining challenge
excerpt:
Andrea Stella has tempered expectations ahead of the Italian Grand Prix, warning that the characteristics which allowed the MCL40 to dominate at the Hungaroring and Zandvoort may count for little at the Temple of Speed.

Lando Norris arrives in Monza on the back of consecutive victories and pole positions, a run that has thrust McLaren firmly into the race-win conversation.

The reigning F1 drivers' champion sits fourth in the standings on 159 points, 83 behind leader Kimi Antonelli, but the momentum is unmistakably with the British driver.

After the Dutch Grand Prix, Antonelli conceded that Mercedes were "clearly not the fastest car any more on the grid," while Norris was bullish on team radio, declaring: "The fight's still on, let's keep going."

Yet Stella is conscious that Monza represents an entirely different test. The Hungaroring and Zandvoort are high-downforce circuits that reward cornering performance and aerodynamic stability, precisely the areas where the MCL40 has excelled since its major upgrade package.

Monza, by contrast, demands the lowest drag configuration of the season, with cars at full throttle for roughly 80 per cent of the lap and heavy braking into tight chicanes.

"The real approach we have is just one race at a time," the McLaren team principal told media, including RacingNews365. "There's not much more you can influence than just maximising what's next available, and the next race will be Monza.

"And if we think about the demand of Zandvoort and Hungary, and then we think about the demand of Monza, we are in a completely different regime.

"So I think if we can confirm our improvements in Monza, then I would say that the answer to your question is, 'Yes, we can look with some optimism at the remainder of the season'."

Drag and braking under the microscope

Norris, for his part, acknowledged that two wins have not masked the MCL40's limitations.

"Despite the win, I'm not fully satisfied," he said after Zandvoort. "We still have weaknesses, particularly in the slow-speed corners, and we need to improve if we want to fight for the championship."

Stella pinpointed the specific areas of concern for Monza, where long straights and hard braking zones will place the MCL40 under a very different kind of scrutiny.

"But first of all, we need to go to Monza and see that our car can express a good performance on the long straights," he added.

"And we know that drag is not necessarily a point of strength of our car, for instance. There's a lot of braking, which is not necessarily a point of strength of our car.

"So there are a lot of things that we need to confirm... But so far, I think we can confirm that when we are at high-downforce circuits with this sort of layout, then we can fight for victories."

title: Max Verstappen 'calms whole system down' as Racing Bulls target 'perfect moment' for driver decision
excerpt:
Racing Bulls CEO Peter Bayer has pointed out that Max Verstappen extending his deal in Milton Keynes "calms the whole system down" given the Dutchman's influence over the F1 driver market, both inside and outside the Red Bull family.

Silly season in the paddock has experienced somewhat of a false start this year, with the four-time F1 drivers' champion joining the Williams pair of Alex Albon and Carlos Sainz in staying put at their current teams.

However, it makes the picture substantially clearer at Racing Bulls, with the Faenza-based squad now able to continue to access its options without the lingering prospect of either Liam Lawson or Arvid Lindblad being called up to partner Isack Hadjar at the top team.

That would have still been an outside possibility, with Red Bull naturally a would-be prospect for whichever driver Verstappen would have replaced elsewhere, in that now-discarded hypothetical.

But it does nonetheless make the equation more straightforward at Racing Bulls, with the team able to choose from its current pairing and F2 drivers' championship leader Nikola Tsolov, who has impressed across the campaign.

The Bulgarian will get his first proper taste of F1 machinery at Imola on Thursday, taking part in a TPC (Testing of Previous Cars) run in last year's VCARB 02.

Whilst the 19-year-old is on the radar of a race seat at the team, there is still a strong chance he slots into the reserve role, given how strongly Lawson and Lindblad are performing, something Bayer was keen to stress.

"Great news on Max, honestly, because that obviously calms the whole system down, and at the same time, we are very happy with both Liam and Arvid and the job they're doing," he told media, including RacingNews365.

Racing Bulls has long said it would take its time making its final call, and Bayer was quick to reiterate that team principal Alan Permane will make that decision when the time is right.

"So we're not in a rush. We have a good pool of drivers coming up through the junior programme," he added in reference to Tsolov.

"So I guess Alan really wants to keep everyone calm, everyone focused, and he will decide when the perfect moment is to inform the drivers and everyone here."
